title: Fridge hacks and Binance expose cyber cover gap as premiums climb
full_text:
Two of the most significant cyber incidents of October 2026 left businesses facing losses their policies did not cover. One was a coordinated attack on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. The other, the largest crypto theft on record. The gap between what companies buy and what pays out is becoming a defining challenge for the cyber insurance market, even as the market grows.
GlobalData, a commercial intelligence firm, forecasts in its Global Insurance Database that global cyber insurance premiums will reach US$16.6 billion in 2026, up 6.9% on the prior year, before accelerating to 10% growth in 2027, taking premiums to US$18.3 billion. The firm attributes the expected acceleration to rising attack frequency, greater business awareness, and wider adoption of internet-connected technology.
GlobalData derives these figures from a proprietary database covering 83 markets. Where direct regulatory data is unavailable, it applies a modelling methodology anchored on each market’s broader general insurance base.
The European refrigeration attack began in France overnight on October 11 to 12 and spread to seven countries, including Ireland and the UK. Hackers raised temperatures to 50°C across approximately 350 supermarkets, forcing chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, and Carrefour to discard fresh and frozen food. Intermarché confirmed to AFP that its insurance did not cover the incident. David Molony, Aon’s head of cyber solutions for EMEA, said most UK retailers lack the specialist endorsement required for perishable goods losses.
Standard cyber policies typically exclude physical losses, while property policies with spoilage cover often carry cyber exclusions. Stock destroyed by a cyberattack on a refrigeration system can fall between both. French authorities have attributed the attack to Iran, according to Al Jazeera, a development with direct implications for coverage disputes. Most cyber policies contain war and state-backed attack exclusions that apply where a government actor is identified.
The same exclusion complications surfaced over the Binance theft. The FBI attributed the US$6.3 billion theft from the cryptocurrency exchange to North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor on October 31. Bloomberg Law reported Binance was unable to obtain cyber insurance, a situation common across crypto firms. Even where crypto firms can find cover, most standard cyber policies exclude fund losses unless a digital asset endorsement is added. The North Korean attribution means a war exclusion could also apply.
“The cover businesses buy does not always match the attacks they face,” said Charlie Hutcherson, senior insurance analyst at GlobalData. “Without clearer protection, businesses risk paying for cover that does not respond when it matters most.”
The two incidents reflect a broader trajectory. Operational technology, the hardware and software that controls physical systems, is increasingly connected to IT networks, creating pathways for attacks that cause physical as well as digital harm. As more OT environments come online, the coverage questions the supermarket attack raised will extend further.
Standard wordings that served clients in a data-breach-focused world may carry exclusions that void cover for attacks on physical systems. Perishable goods endorsements, digital asset cover, and clarity on war exclusion triggers have moved from specialist edge cases to renewal-table questions.
Hutcherson noted that insurers offering clearer wordings and specialist endorsements will be best placed to capture the premium growth expected over 2026 and 2027.
